title: How Agentic AI Will Reshape Payments (IMF Notes 2026/004)
key_claim: The note examines agentic AI across authorization, liquidity, settlement, compliance and resilience, and identifies a key tension between probabilistic AI behaviour and the deterministic requirements of payment infrastructures, using an intent / authorization / settlement three-layer analysis.
frame_summary: Argues that payment systems should preserve deterministic control and finality while agentic capability is layered on top; its three-layer intent-authorization-settlement device exists to keep probabilistic agents away from settlement, and it holds that outcomes depend on institutional design and governance as much as technology.
verbatim_quote: It highlights a key tension between probabilistic AI behavior and the deterministic requirements of payment infrastructures.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band): canonical multilateral framing of agent-mediated payments, published 24/04/2026. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 29/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

publisher: Office of U.S. Senator Mark R. Warner
title: Warner Unveils Discussion Draft of Legislation to Create Innovative Market for Secure Artificial Intelligence Agents
key_claim: On 29 June 2026 Senator Warner released a discussion draft of the AI AGENT Act: a federal framework with an FTC registry of trusted AI agents, NIST standards work on authentication, and guaranteed secure agent access to large online platforms, released for stakeholder feedback before formal introduction.
frame_summary: Argues the consumer-agent market needs a federal access-and-trust framework built around consumer choice and fair competition, and that the right sequence is a discussion draft refined by stakeholder feedback before a bill is introduced.
verbatim_quote: The AI AGENT Act would establish a federal framework to protect consumer choice, promote fair competition, and ensure AI agents operate in the best interests of the users they represent.
verbatim_list: Direct NIST to identify technical standards and open protocols to make online services more accessible to AI agents and to ensure consensus-based standards around critical mechanisms like authentication.
notes: Tier 1 legislative primary. The quoted sentence carries inline italics around 'AI AGENT Act' on the live page; span verified by hand during the 29/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: Financial Stability Report - July 2026
key_claim: The July 2026 Financial Stability Report says longer-reasoning agentic applications raise usage-based costs, and that Bank staff are currently undertaking deep dives on agentic payments and agentic trading, alongside Project Logos with the BIS Innovation Hub simulating LLM-based agents in financial markets.
frame_summary: Argues frontier-AI progress raises UK financial stability risk mainly through cyber and operational channels, and treats agentic finance as a subject for study: the Bank is at the deep-dive and simulation stage, not the rule-setting stage.
verbatim_quote: Bank staff are therefore currently undertaking deep dives on agentic payments and agentic trading.
verbatim_list: To explore these risks, the Bank is working with the BIS Innovation Hub London Centre and other stakeholders on Project Logos, which aims to enable central banks to observe and analyse the behaviour of large language model (LLM)-based agents acting as portfolio managers in a simulated financial market environment.
notes: Tier 1 central-bank primary. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 29/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: Agentic AI and Consumer Protection (issue paper by Christoph Busch)
date_evidence: July 16, 2026 (visible dateline under title); og:image path /wp-content/uploads/2026/07/
key_claim: EU consumer law implicitly assumes the person making the purchasing decision is a human being; consent, disclosure and liability rules do not map onto agent transactions, and some estimates suggest 10% to 20% of e-commerce transactions could be handled by an AI agent by 2030.
frame_summary: Argues EU consumer law breaks once an agent sits between consumer and trader, and that the Digital Fairness Act (expected Q3 2026) should settle contract validity, shift to compliance-by-protocol and differentiate agent types; frames intervening too late as now a greater risk than intervening too early.
verbatim_quote: When an agent buys the wrong product or authorises a payment it should not have, existing rules say little about how the risk should fall between consumer, agent provider and trader.
verbatim_list: Some estimates suggest that between 10% and 20% of e-commerce transactions could be handled by an AI agent by 2030.
The Digital Fairness Act, expected in the third quarter of 2026, offers the opportunity to respond.
Without a clear liability architecture, the paper warns, consumers have little reason to trust delegated decision-making, and providers little incentive to offer it.
notes: Tier 2 institutional research (Brussels regulatory think-tank; author is Professor of Law, University of Osnabrück). Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 29/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: New York's financial regulator turns its attention to agentic commerce
key_claim: At the New York Fed's Innovation Conference on 26 June, NYDFS acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow flagged unresolved risks as consumers begin transacting through AI agents; the Department has not settled its expectations for allocation of agentic transaction liability.
frame_summary: Argues Asrow's remarks show state regulators will carry existing consumer-protection expectations into agentic commerce, with accountability expected to land on the regulated entity offering the product rather than the software that arranged it, while formal expectations remain unsettled and states move ahead of any national standard.
verbatim_quote: The Department has not settled its expectations for allocation of agentic transaction liability.
verbatim_list: Speaking at the New York Federal Reserve's Innovation Conference on June 26, New York Department of Financial Services (the Department) acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow signaled that her agency is watching the rise of agentic commerce closely and is working through how its long-standing consumer protections should apply.
notes: Tier 3 law-firm client alert reporting a primary regulator's public remarks; no NYDFS transcript of the 26 June remarks is published, so the alert is the best available record. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 29/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: AI shopping agents are coming. No one is ready for them
date_evidence: June 12, 2026, 8:08 PM ET (visible dateline under byline)
key_claim: A Fortune Brainstorm Tech panel concluded no one is ready for AI shopping agents: liability is being negotiated company to company with no standards, and OpenAI has pivoted away from its Instant Checkout feature, with initial retailers such as Walmart pulling out.
frame_summary: Argues the industry consensus is that agentic shopping lacks the standards it needs on security, fraud, refunds and liability, and that consumer demand will force adoption before those solutions exist.
verbatim_quote: Liability is wide open right now and being negotiated company to company, but there are no standards around where liability sits when an agent buys something that maybe the user didn’t intend or ask for.
verbatim_list: She noted that even when a user asks ChatGPT about a product type it might want to purchase, such as ski gloves, it responds with specific product recommendations only 9% of the time.

She said she thought OpenAI had fumbled its initial efforts to build its chatbot into a commerce platform, pivoting away from its Instant Checkout feature that allowed a user to complete a purchase directly from the chat interface.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism. The verbatim quote is Courtney Robinson (Akoya) as quoted by Fortune. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 29/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: Agentic commerce liability is still being written
key_claim: Visa, Mastercard and American Express have all launched agent transaction frameworks and EMVCo has stood up a dedicated agentic payments task force, but no liability shift exists yet: disputes short of outright fraud have no clean answer, and Regulation E assumes binary authorization.
frame_summary: Argues fraud liability is largely handled by existing tokenized-transaction rules while dispute allocation short of fraud is unresolved, and that merchants should build agent identity, intent-verification and credential controls now, with the card networks the only actors able to close the liability gap at scale.
verbatim_quote: A shopper who claims their agent misunderstood an instruction, bought the wrong item or acted outside what they authorized is making a dispute claim, not a fraud claim.
verbatim_list: Worldpay’s Agentic Commerce Report found 45% of consumers were ready to let an AI agent complete a purchase on their behalf, rising to 54% among Gen Z. At the same time, 95% reported at least one concern about agentic commerce, and 50% said fraud protections in place would make them trust it more.
Visa’s Intelligent Commerce Connect launched in April 2026, giving agent platforms a single integration point for onboarding, verification and token issuance across major agent protocols.

EMVCo, the body that maintains the global EMV specifications underlying card payments, has also started work in this space, standing up a dedicated task force to explore how its specifications could eventually support agentic payments.
notes: Tier 4 vendor source (payment processor; author leads its agentic commerce line) - treat directionally; used for the card-network framework timeline and its own consumer survey, corroborated by Tier 1-3 sources on the liability gap itself. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 29/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.
